title: Russia’s Turn to China Under Sanctions: Sanctions Decay, Substitution Elasticity, and the Challenge of Sustaining Pressure
gist: CSIS's Damien Spleeters argues Western export controls on Russia are judged wrongly by component displacement: Russia has shifted to Chinese supply (about 75% of priority-goods exports, paying a ~300% premium) while drone and missile use rose. He proposes measuring 'substitution elasticity' and capability disruption, warning that sanctions decay as US enforcement stalls and China's new counter-sanctions order reduces visibility.

insights.claim: Ukraine's sanctions commissioner said in May 2026 that Russia's forced shift from Western to Chinese components showed sanctions working, yet Russia's missile and drone use had increased year over year.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Component displacement does not equal reduced Russian military output; war intensity persists.
insights.quote: Controls may displace Western components and impose real costs without sufficiently reducing Russia’s ability to produce and deploy weapons.

insights.claim: US continuous sanctions implementation against Russia has largely stalled while the EU and UK keep adding designations, such as the EU's 21st package in July 2026 with 37 drone-linked listings and 51 entities added to dual-use restrictions, including Chinese and Hong Kong firms.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Transatlantic divergence on Russia sanctions raises compliance complexity and secondary-sanction risk for Chinese firms in Europe.
insights.locator: The political context makes the problem more urgent

insights.claim: Sanctions decay is the progressive loss of a restriction's practical effect; its pace depends on substitution elasticity, defined as the speed, cost, engineering burden, performance penalty, reliability loss and visibility change of replacing a restricted item or route.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A usable lens for judging which export controls actually bite.
insights.quote: That progressive loss of practical effect is known as sanctions decay.

insights.claim: The Kyiv School of Economics found export controls since 2022 cut the value of Russia's Common High Priority imports by more than half, but China now supplies roughly 75 percent of those goods to Russia.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Russia's military supply chain is now concentrated on China, giving Beijing leverage.

insights.claim: KSE found the premium Russia paid China for priority dual-use goods rose with its dependence and reached about 300 percent in 2025.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Chinese intermediaries extract large rents from sanctioned Russian demand.

insights.claim: The author argues a price premium is evidence of friction but not by itself evidence of capability disruption, so sanctions should not be declared either working or failing based on it.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Investors should discount simplistic sanctions-success narratives when assessing war duration.
insights.quote: A price increase is evidence of friction, but it is not, by itself, evidence of capability disruption.
insights.locator: Those findings should not be reduced

insights.claim: Chinese actors support Russia in three distinct ways: diverting Western technology through concealed chains, supplying Chinese-made substitutes, and helping Russia integrate and produce capabilities, each changing jurisdiction and leverage.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Western leverage shrinks as support moves from diversion to Chinese substitution and co-production.
insights.locator: Through China, From China, and With China

insights.claim: Ukrainian intelligence records show Russia's Geran-4 drone uses a Chinese turbojet engine, network switch, mesh modem and transceiver alongside US-made components, evidencing mixed sourcing rather than full replacement.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Western components still leak into Russian weapons, sustaining enforcement exposure for Western chipmakers.

insights.claim: In 2024 the US Treasury sanctioned Chinese entities involved in the Garpiya long-range attack drone, its first sanctions on Chinese entities directly developing and producing complete weapons systems with Russian firms.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Marks escalation of China's role from supplier to co-producer, raising secondary sanctions risk.

insights.claim: A Geran-2 drone used in 2025 carried a new anti-jamming navigation antenna with 15 identified components, only two American, including a signal-processing chip from the Beijing Microelectronics Technology Institute.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Chinese defense electronics are substituting into critical Russian navigation subsystems.

insights.claim: Avinex Global registered in Hong Kong one week before the US added affiliate Avtex Semiconductor to the Entity List, and later sent thousands of microelectronics shipments to Russia, showing how successor entities preempt name-based sanctions.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Name-based designations decay quickly; compliance screening must track networks, not names.

insights.claim: China's State Council Order No. 834 (2026) allows countermeasures against foreign organizations that interrupt normal transactions with Chinese entities and subjects supply chain investigations conducted in China to Chinese law.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Western firms doing sanctions due diligence in China face legal retaliation risk, raising compliance cost.
insights.locator: China is also changing the legal environment

insights.claim: The author argues China's expanding counter-sanctions framework may raise the cost of sanctions-driven disengagement and reduce visibility into substitute suppliers and routes.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Decoupling from Chinese suppliers becomes costlier for multinationals.
insights.locator: China is also changing the legal environment

insights.claim: The author recommends requiring substitution assessments before major controls, identifying likely Chinese alternatives, integration time, performance penalties and observable indicators.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Could make future export controls more targeted at chokepoints like machine tools and test equipment.

insights.claim: Durable leverage may lie less in interchangeable components than in inelastic dependencies such as software, machine tools, test equipment, materials, carrier boards, logistics firms, finance and insurance.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Points to future control targets: machine tools, semiconductor equipment, logistics and financial intermediaries.

insights.claim: Mass tracing of many recovered components and triangulation of recurring distributors can identify acquisition channels before they become durable workarounds.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Distributors repeatedly appearing in trace results face elevated enforcement risk.

insights.claim: For genuine Chinese substitutes, allied leverage is narrower, and the author warns against pretending every supply chain contains a Western switch that can be turned off.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Limits expectations that tighter Western controls alone can degrade Russian war production.
insights.quote: The answer is not to pretend that every supply chain contains a Western switch that can be turned off.

insights.claim: Controls should be judged by whether the adversary's capability became slower, costlier, less reliable, harder to scale or more visible, not by the nationality of recovered components.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Reframes how to read sanctions effectiveness claims from governments.
insights.quote: Controls should be judged by whether the adversary’s capability became slower, costlier, less reliable, harder to scale, or more visible.
